title: 0-1 BFS
html:
It is well-known, that you can find the shortest paths between a single source and all other vertices in O(∣E∣)O(|E|)O(∣E∣) using Breadth First Search in an unweighted graph, i.e. the distance is the minimal number of edges that you need to traverse from the source to another vertex. We can interpret such a graph also as a weighted graph, where every edge has the weight 111. If not all edges in graph have the same weight, then we need a more general algorithm, like Dijkstra which runs in O(∣V∣2+∣E∣)O(|V|^2 + |E|)O(∣V∣2+∣E∣) or O(∣E∣log⁡∣V∣)O(|E| \log |V|)O(∣E∣log∣V∣) time.

However if the weights are more constrained, we can often do better. In this article we demonstrate how we can use BFS to solve the SSSP (single-source shortest path) problem in O(∣E∣)O(|E|)O(∣E∣), if the weight of each edge is either 000 or 111.

Algorithm

We can develop the algorithm by closely studying Dijkstra's algorithm and thinking about the consequences that our special graph implies. The general form of Dijkstra's algorithm is (here a set is used for the priority queue):

d.assign(n, INF);
d[s] = 0;
set<pair<int, int>> q;
q.insert({0, s});
while (!q.empty()) {
    int v = q.begin()->second;
    q.erase(q.begin());

    for (auto edge : adj[v]) {
        int u = edge.first;
        int w = edge.second;

        if (d[v] + w < d[u]) {
            q.erase({d[u], u});
            d[u] = d[v] + w;
            q.insert({d[u], u});
        }
    }
}

We can notice that the difference between the distances between the source s and two other vertices in the queue differs by at most one. Especially, we know that d[v]≤d[u]≤d[v]+1d[v] \le d[u] \le d[v] + 1d[v]≤d[u]≤d[v]+1 for each u∈Qu \in Qu∈Q. The reason for this is, that we only add vertices with equal distance or with distance plus one to the queue during each iteration. Assuming there exists a uuu in the queue with d[u]−d[v]>1d[u] - d[v] > 1d[u]−d[v]>1, then uuu must have been inserted into the queue via a different vertex ttt with d[t]≥d[u]−1>d[v]d[t] \ge d[u] - 1 > d[v]d[t]≥d[u]−1>d[v]. However this is impossible, since Dijkstra's algorithm iterates over the vertices in increasing order.

This means, that the order of the queue looks like this:

Q=v⏟d[v],…,u⏟d[v],m⏟d[v]+1…n⏟d[v]+1Q = \underbrace{v}_{d[v]}, \dots, \underbrace{u}_{d[v]}, \underbrace{m}_{d[v]+1} \dots \underbrace{n}_{d[v]+1}Q=d[v]v​​,…,d[v]u​​,d[v]+1m​​…d[v]+1n​​

This structure is so simple, that we don't need an actual priority queue, i.e. using a balanced binary tree would be an overkill. Since the queue only ever holds two distinct distances, we can keep them in two separate vectors: q0q_0q0​ for the vertices at distance d[v]d[v]d[v], and q1q_1q1​ for those at distance d[v]+1d[v] + 1d[v]+1. An edge of weight 000 appends to q0q_0q0​, an edge of weight 111 to q1q_1q1​. Once q0q_0q0​ runs out, every vertex at the current distance has been processed, so we swap the two vectors and the current distance increases by one.

vector<int> d(n, INF);
d[s] = 0;
vector<int> q0, q1;
q0.push_back(s);
while (!q0.empty()) {
    int v = q0.back();
    q0.pop_back();
    for (auto edge : adj[v]) {
        int u = edge.first;
        int w = edge.second;
        if (d[v] + w < d[u]) {
            d[u] = d[v] + w;
            if (w == 0)
                q0.push_back(u);
            else
                q1.push_back(u);
        }
    }
    if (q0.empty())
        swap(q0, q1);
}

Written this way the two levels are explicit: a vertex is appended to q0q_0q0​ when it is reached at the current distance and to q1q_1q1​ when it is reached one step further, so the structure of QQQ shown above is built into the code rather than maintained by hand. A vertex that was appended to q1q_1q1​ and is then improved to the current distance leaves its old copy behind, but the stale copy is harmless: when it is finally popped, the test d[v] + w < d[u] finds nothing left to improve. Note that q0q_0q0​ is used as a stack rather than a queue, which is harmless: all of its vertices share the same distance, so the order in which they are processed does not matter.

The same algorithm is more commonly written with a single deque, pushing to the front for weight 000 and to the back for weight 111, so that push_front and push_back play the roles of q0q_0q0​ and q1q_1q1​. Two vectors are preferable in practice because they avoid the deque's chunked storage: on graphs small enough to stay in cache this measures about 1.151.151.15 times faster, falling to roughly 1.061.061.06 times on graphs of millions of vertices, where memory latency dominates and the choice of container matters much less (see this benchmark).

If no edge has weight 000, the algorithm degenerates into an ordinary BFS, and in that case a plain BFS is both simpler and slightly faster.

Dial's algorithm

We can extend this even further if we allow the weights of the edges to be even bigger. If every edge in the graph has a weight ≤k\le k≤k, then the distances of vertices in the queue will differ by at most kkk from the distance of vvv to the source. So we can keep k+1k + 1k+1 buckets for the vertices in the queue, and whenever the bucket corresponding to the smallest distance gets empty, we make a cyclic shift to get the bucket with the next higher distance. This extension is called Dial's algorithm.
